title: Chapter XXIV

teacherSummary.text: Walton resumes writing. The ice traps the ship; the crew demands to turn south, and Walton yields. Victor dies. The creature appears over his body, mourns, condemns himself, and vows to destroy himself on a funeral pyre before vanishing into darkness.

vocabulary.context: You have read this strange and terrific story, Margaret; and do you not feel your blood congeal with horror, like that which even now curdles mine?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “curdle”: cur (Latin cura, "care"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To free from encumbrance, or from anything which clogs, impedes, or obstructs
vocabulary.context: But this was not the time for delay: I disencumbered the dogs of their dead companion, gave them a plentiful portion of food; and, after an hour’s rest, which was absolutely necessary, and yet which was bitterly irksome to me, I continued my route.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “disencumber”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not") + -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To denounce evil against, or to imprecate evil upon
vocabulary.context: Why do you not execrate the rustic who sought to destroy the saviour of his child?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “execrate”: ex- (Latin ex, "out of") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The act of giving premature birth
vocabulary.context: I, the miserable and the abandoned, am an abortion, to be spurned at, and kicked, and trampled on.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “abortion”: ab- (Latin ab, "away from"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To change from a fluid to a solid state by cold
vocabulary.context: You have read this strange and terrific story, Margaret; and do you not feel your blood congeal with horror, like that which even now curdles mine?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “congeal”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To give feeble or scattered rays of light
vocabulary.context: Frankenstein has daily declined in health: a feverish fire still glimmers in his eyes; but he is exhausted, and, when suddenly roused to any exertion, he speedily sinks again into apparent lifelessness.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “glimmer”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: A mark in the skin or flesh of an animal, made by a wound or ulcer, and remaining after the wound or ulcer is healed
vocabulary.context: I approached this tremendous being; I dared not again raise my eyes to his face, there was something so scaring and unearthly in his ugliness.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “scar”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: You will find near this place, if you follow not too tardily, a dead hare; eat, and be refreshed.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “tardily”: ard (Latin ardere, "to burn") + -ly (Old English -lice, "in the manner of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To form by putting together two or more things or parts
vocabulary.context: Oh, no! the only joy that he can now know will be when he composes his shattered spirit to peace and death.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “compose”: com- (Latin com-, "with, together") + pos (Latin ponere, "to place"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To form, as sound, to a certain key, or to a certain portion
vocabulary.context: He spoke this with a voice so modulated to the different feelings expressed in his speech, with an eye so full of lofty design and heroism, that can you wonder that these men were moved?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “modulate”: -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Walton's choice to return is a moral decision, contrasting with Victor's refusal to stop.

significance: The ending lets Walton learn the lesson, while the creature's final speech gives him the last eloquent word.
discussionQuestions: Does Walton learn from Victor? What evidence shows it?
Where does point of view appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with the sublime power of nature?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXIV,” how does Shelley show the final reckoning? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the point of view you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XXIV, how does Shelley develop the idea of the final reckoning? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the point of view in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXIV develops the idea of the final reckoning. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XXIV (where it begins, turns and ends) and its point of view shape the reader's understanding of the final reckoning. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XXIV suggests about the final reckoning. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's point of view and theme), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses point of view in Chapter XXIV to complicate the reader's understanding of the final reckoning. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXIV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the final reckoning responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XXIV alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of the final reckoning follows or bends those conventions, using the point of view as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XXIV and its treatment of the final reckoning. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's point of view and theme, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XXIV as evidence for a larger claim about the final reckoning in Frankenstein. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXIV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the final reckoning. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

satQuestions.passage: What his feelings were whom I pursued I cannot know. Sometimes, indeed, he left marks in writing on the barks of the trees, or cut in stone, that guided me, and instigated my fury. “My reign is not yet over,” (these words were legible in one of these inscriptions;) “you live, and my power is complete. Follow me; I seek the everlasting ices of the north, where you will feel the misery of cold and frost, to which I am impassive. You will find near this place, if you follow not too tardily, a dead hare; eat, and be refreshed. Come on, my enemy; we have yet to wrestle for our lives; but many hard and miserable hours must you endure until that period shall arrive.”
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XXIV”?

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Does Walton learn from Victor? What evidence shows it? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are curdles, disencumbered, execrate, abortion, congeal. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “You have read this strange and terrific story, Margaret; and do you not feel your blood congeal with horror, like that which even now curdles mine?” Webster's says: To change into curd. Now the word history: “curdle”: cur (Latin cura, "care"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “disencumber”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not") + -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “execrate”: ex- (Latin ex, "out of") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Walton's choice to return is a moral decision, contrasting with Victor's refusal to stop. Why does this chapter matter? The ending lets Walton learn the lesson, while the creature's final speech gives him the last eloquent word. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for point of view.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see point of view, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to the final reckoning.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Point of view, Theme, Irony.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of point of view. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

Follow me; I seek the everlasting ices of the north, where you will feel the misery of cold and frost, to which I am impassive. segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Point of view, Theme, Irony: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XXIV,” how does Shelley show the final reckoning? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the point of view you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about the final reckoning, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how point of view shapes the final reckoning. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
